title: Advanced String Processing & Regex
summary: Beyond basic substitution — bash regex, heredocs, printf formatting, and the text-processing patterns that show up in every real DevOps script.

sections.title: Bash regex with [[ =~ ]]
sections.body:
## Bash Regex: Pattern Matching Without a Subprocess

Regular expressions are one of the most powerful pattern-matching tools in computing. In DevOps scripting, you use them constantly: validating that a string is a valid AWS region, checking that an image tag follows a semantic versioning format, extracting a version number from a release artifact name, or detecting whether an image reference includes a specific tag. The instinct is often to pipe the string through `grep -E` or `sed -E` to apply the regex — and that works, but it spawns a new process for what is fundamentally an in-memory string operation.

Bash's `[[ =~ ]]` operator brings extended regular expression matching directly into the shell. When a string matches the pattern, bash sets the `BASH_REMATCH` array: `BASH_REMATCH[0]` contains the full match, and `BASH_REMATCH[1]`, `[2]`, etc. contain the content of each capture group in parentheses. This makes it possible to both test for a match and extract specific parts of the matched string in a single operation — without forking a subprocess.

The performance difference matters in loops. If you are processing 500 pod names to check whether each follows a naming convention, `[[ =~ ]]` is significantly faster than piping each name to `grep`. But the more important benefit is clarity: keeping the regex test in the shell condition (`if [[ "$str" =~ pattern ]]; then`) makes the intent of the code immediately obvious without the distraction of a subprocess invocation.

One syntax note: **do not quote the regex pattern** in `[[ =~ ]]`. Quoting forces a literal string match instead of a regex match — a common gotcha that results in `[[ "v1.2.3" =~ "^v[0-9]+" ]]` always being false. The pattern should be unquoted or stored in a variable.

**Why:** avoid spawning grep just to check if a string matches a pattern. `[[ =~ ]]` runs regex in the current shell and captures groups via `BASH_REMATCH`.

```bash
# Basic match
version="v1.35.0"
if [[ "$version" =~ ^v([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)$ ]]; then
    major="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
    minor="${BASH_REMATCH[2]}"
    patch="${BASH_REMATCH[3]}"
    echo "Major: $major, Minor: $minor, Patch: $patch"
fi

# Validate AWS region format
validate_region() {
    local region="$1"
    if [[ ! "$region" =~ ^[a-z]{2}-[a-z]+-[0-9]$ ]]; then
        echo "ERROR: invalid region format: $region" >&2
        return 1
    fi
}

validate_region "eu-central-1"   # OK
validate_region "eu-central"     # ERROR

# Extract image tag from full image string
image="123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/my-app:v1.2.3"
if [[ "$image" =~ :([^:]+)$ ]]; then
    tag="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"   # v1.2.3
fi

# Check for 'latest' or missing tag (dangerous in prod)
if [[ "$image" =~ :latest$ ]] || [[ ! "$image" =~ : ]]; then
    echo "WARNING: image not pinned to a specific version"
fi

# Extract k8s resource from kubectl error
error="Error from server (NotFound): pods \"my-pod\" not found"
if [[ "$error" =~ \"([^\"]+)\" ]]; then
    resource_name="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
fi
```

sections.title: printf for proper formatting
sections.body:
## printf: Precise, Portable Output Formatting

Output formatting is often an afterthought in bash scripts, but it has a real operational impact. A script that produces neatly aligned, consistently formatted output is dramatically easier to scan during an incident than one that produces ragged, inconsistent text. When you are looking at a wall of pod status output at 2am, the difference between a formatted table and an unformatted stream is the difference between spotting the problem in seconds and spending minutes parsing the output manually.

`echo` is the obvious choice for output, but it has a significant portability problem: the behavior of `echo -e` (interpreting escape sequences like `\n` and `\t`) and `echo -n` (suppressing the trailing newline) varies between bash versions and between bash and dash (which is often the default `/bin/sh` on Debian-based systems). A script that works correctly on macOS may produce garbled output on a CI runner using Ubuntu because `echo` behaves differently.

`printf` solves this. It is specified by POSIX, behaves identically across platforms, and has a format string syntax (borrowed from C) that gives you precise control over field widths, alignment, padding, and number formatting. The format string `%-30s %-15s %5d\n` produces a left-aligned 30-character string field, a left-aligned 15-character string field, a right-aligned 5-character integer field, and a newline — consistently, on every platform.

For DevOps output specifically, `printf` enables the kind of aligned table formatting that makes status reports legible: pod names in a fixed-width column, statuses in a fixed-width column, restart counts in a right-aligned numeric column. Combined with ANSI color codes for highlighting problem rows, `printf`-formatted output from a health check script is something you actually want to look at.

**Why:** `echo` is inconsistent across platforms (`-e`, `-n` behave differently). `printf` is POSIX, predictable, and much more powerful for formatted output.

```bash
# Basic formatting
printf "%-30s %-15s %s\n" "NAME" "STATUS" "AGE"    # left-aligned columns
printf "%30s %15s %5s\n"  "NAME" "STATUS" "AGE"    # right-aligned
printf "%-30s %-15s %5d\n" "my-pod" "Running" 42   # integer formatting

# Colours without echo -e
RED="\033[31m"; GREEN="\033[32m"; RESET="\033[0m"
printf "%bFAILED%b: %s\n" "$RED" "$RESET" "pod crashed"

# Writing to files safely (no trailing newline issues)
printf '%s\n' "line1" "line2" "line3" > output.txt

# Zero-padded numbers
for i in $(seq 1 5); do
    printf "job-%03d\n" "$i"   # job-001, job-002 ...
done

# Table output — real-world pod status
print_pod_table() {
    printf "\n%-55s %-20s %-10s %s\n" "NAME" "STATUS" "RESTARTS" "AGE"
    printf '%s\n' "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..100})"
    while IFS='|' read -r name status restarts age; do
        if [[ "$status" != "Running" ]]; then
            printf "${RED}%-55s %-20s %-10s %s${RESET}\n" "$name" "$status" "$restarts" "$age"
        else
            printf "${GREEN}%-55s${RESET} %-20s %-10s %s\n" "$name" "$status" "$restarts" "$age"
        fi
    done
}
```

sections.title: Heredocs and herestrings
sections.body:
## Heredocs and Herestrings: Embedding Multi-Line Content in Scripts

Bash scripts frequently need to work with multi-line content: Kubernetes manifests, YAML configuration files, SQL queries, JSON templates, shell script snippets to be written to a file. The naive approach — echoing each line separately or using escaped newlines inside a string — is fragile and hard to read. Heredocs are the right tool for this.

A heredoc lets you embed a block of text directly in a script, with the content delimited by a word of your choice (conventionally `EOF`). Between the opening `<< EOF` and the closing `EOF` line, you write the content exactly as you want it to appear — newlines, indentation, and all — without any quoting or escaping. The shell passes this content to the command (often `cat`, `kubectl apply -f -`, or `tee`) as its standard input.

The two most important heredoc variants are **unquoted** (`<< EOF`) and **quoted** (`<< 'EOF'`). Unquoted heredocs expand variables and command substitutions inside the content — useful for generating manifests with environment-specific values. Quoted heredocs treat everything literally — essential when generating scripts or configs that contain dollar signs that should not be expanded (like another script's variable references, or PromQL queries).

Herestrings (`<<< "string"`) are a lighter-weight variant for single values. `read -r first rest <<< "hello world"` splits a string into parts without creating a subshell. `jq . <<< "$json_var"` processes a JSON string without a temporary file. Like process substitution, herestrings avoid the subshell problem that comes with pipes, making them useful when you need to preserve variable assignments.

In Kubernetes automation, heredocs appear most often in scripts that generate manifests on the fly — where the manifest content includes values from the environment (image tags, namespace names, resource limits) that are known at runtime but not at script-write time.

```bash
# Basic heredoc — preserves newlines, expands variables
cat << EOF
Namespace: $NAMESPACE
Context:   $(kubectl config current-context)
Date:      $(date -u)
EOF

# Quoted heredoc — no variable expansion (literal)
cat << 'EOF'
This $VARIABLE will NOT be expanded.
Neither will $(this command).
EOF

# Indented heredoc (bash 4+, use tab for indent)
if true; then
    cat <<- EOF
        This content has leading tabs stripped.
        Useful inside indented if/for blocks.
    EOF
fi

# Heredoc to a file
cat > /tmp/manifest.yaml << EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: ${APP_NAME}-config
  namespace: ${NAMESPACE}
data:
  environment: ${ENV}
  region: ${AWS_REGION}
EOF

# Heredoc to kubectl apply
kubectl apply -f - << EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: ${NAMESPACE}
  labels:
    managed-by: script
EOF

# Herestring — single line, no subshell
read -r first rest <<< "hello world"
echo "$first"   # hello
echo "$rest"    # world

# Pass JSON to jq without a file
jq -r '.items[].name' <<< '{"items":[{"name":"a"},{"name":"b"}]}'
```

sections.title: Cheat sheet
sections.body:
## Quick Reference: Regex, printf, Heredocs, and String Operations

This cheat sheet brings together the syntax from all three lesson sections into a single scannable reference. The regex section is particularly worth bookmarking — the `BASH_REMATCH` array and the quoting rules for the pattern are easy to forget. The `printf` format string section covers the specifiers you will use in 95% of table-formatting situations. The heredoc variants are distinct enough that confusing them causes mysterious bugs, so the one-line descriptions are worth memorizing.

The string operations at the bottom of the cheat sheet are a condensed version of the parameter expansion operators from the Week 1 quoting lesson — included here because they interact naturally with regex and printf workflows, and having them on the same reference page makes the overall picture clearer.

```bash
# ── Regex ────────────────────────────────────────
[[ "$str" =~ pattern ]]      # match (extended regex)
${BASH_REMATCH[0]}           # full match
${BASH_REMATCH[1]}           # first capture group
[[ "$str" =~ ^v[0-9]+\. ]]  # starts with vN.
[[ ! "$str" =~ latest ]]    # does NOT contain 'latest'

# ── printf format strings ────────────────────────
%-30s   # left-aligned string, 30 wide
%30s    # right-aligned string, 30 wide
%05d    # integer, zero-padded to 5 digits
%8.2f   # float, 8 wide, 2 decimal places
%b      # interpret backslash escapes (for colours)
\n      # newline  \t tab

# ── Heredoc variants ─────────────────────────────
cat << EOF        # expand vars
cat << 'EOF'      # no expansion (literal)
cat <<- EOF       # strip leading TABS (not spaces)
cmd <<< "string" # herestring (single value)

# ── String ops quick ref ─────────────────────────
${#str}              # length
${str:0:5}           # substring from 0, length 5
${str##*/}           # strip longest prefix matching */
${str%.*}            # strip shortest suffix matching .*
${str/old/new}       # replace first
${str//old/new}      # replace all
${str^^}             # uppercase
${str,,}             # lowercase
${str:-default}      # default if unset/empty
${str:?"error msg"}  # error and exit if unset/empty
```

sections.title: Quiz
sections.body:
## Knowledge Check: String Processing, Regex, printf, and Heredocs

This quiz tests the practical understanding built up through the week's lessons. The questions focus on the concepts that have the highest leverage in real scripts: the regex quoting rule (unquoted patterns vs quoted patterns), the difference between heredoc variants, the reasons to prefer `printf` over `echo`, and the mechanics of `BASH_REMATCH`. The exercises at the end give you concrete patterns to try in the terminal — working through them is the fastest way to build muscle memory for these tools.

**Q1.** Given `image="my-app:v1.2.3"`, write a one-liner using `[[ =~ ]]` to extract the tag into `$tag`.

**Q2.** What's the difference between `<< EOF` and `<< 'EOF'`?

**Q3.** Why use `printf` instead of `echo` in scripts?

**Q4.** What does `${str##*/}` do? Give a concrete example.

---

**Answers:**

**A1.** `[[ "$image" =~ :(.+)$ ]] && tag="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"`

**A2.** Unquoted `EOF` expands variables and `$(...)`. Quoted `'EOF'` treats everything literally — useful for generating scripts or configs that contain `$` themselves.

**A3.** `echo` behaviour varies across shells and platforms (`-e`, `-n` are not POSIX). `printf` is consistent, supports format strings, and doesn't add unexpected newlines or interpret escape sequences unless you ask.

**A4.** Strips the longest match of `*/` from the start — effectively gets the filename from a path. `str="/path/to/file.yaml"` → `${str##*/}` = `file.yaml`.

---

**Exercise:**

```bash
# 1. Validate these image strings — flag anything unpinned or using 'latest'
images=(
    "nginx:latest"
    "my-app:v1.2.3"
    "busybox"
    "registry.k8s.io/coredns:1.11.1"
    "my-app:"
)

for image in "${images[@]}"; do
    # TODO: use [[ =~ ]] to detect: no tag, 'latest' tag, or empty tag
    echo "Checking: $image"
done

# 2. Generate a kubeconfig snippet using a heredoc
# with variables for cluster name, endpoint, and namespace
CLUSTER_NAME="eks-prod-mach-x7kq"
ENDPOINT="https://ABCDEF.gr7.eu-central-1.eks.amazonaws.com"
NAMESPACE="argocd"

cat << EOF
# TODO: write the heredoc here
EOF
```
